sentences.text: The name Stellasaurus means "star lizard," a reference to the star-like pattern on its head and the David Bowie song "Starman."
This ceratopsid dinosaur featured complex cranial ornamentation, including a very long nasal horn that was larger than those found in Centrosaurus.
The nasal horn stood erect, curved inward, and was compressed on the sides.
The skull roof displayed long, straight third and fourth spines, while the fifth through seventh spines remained short.
No separate frill ossifications, such as epiparietals or episquamosals, have been discovered, suggesting these genera may have lacked them entirely.
Fossil remains were found in Montana, USA, within the Late Campanian Two Medicine Formation of the Upper Cretaceous.
In 2020, a re-evaluation questioned the previous referral and named it a distinct species in a new genus.
The describers view it as a transitional form between Styracosaurus albertensis and Einiosaurus on a lineage leading to Achelousaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
The authors described the animal as a transitional form between Styracosaurus and Einiosaurus within a single evolutionary line leading to Achelousaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
Stellasaurus is classified in the class Ornithischia.
The animal belongs to the family Ceratopsidae.
Its parent group is the subfamily Centrosaurinae.
The type and only known species is Stellasaurus ancellae.
It lived approximately 75 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now North America.
Stellasaurus lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
Contemporary dinosaurs included hadrosaurids, ankylosaurs, the tyrannosaurid Daspletosaurus, and smaller theropods.
Researchers differ in their interpretation of the fossil, specifically regarding the position of the neck shield and parietal spines.
There is a debate regarding the count of epiparietalia, with Andrew McDonald identifying P8 and Wilson et al. identifying P7.
Wilson et al. do not consider separate skin ossifications, or osteoderms, to have been demonstrated in Styracosaurus, Stellasaurus, and Einiosaurus.
The authors reject the interpretation that ceratopsid evolution in these formations occurred as a succession of branching divisions.
It is debated whether the argument for a direct lineage is more probable than branching models, as critics argue that ancestors and extinction are implied in branching models anyway.
